prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "HSBC HOLDINGS PLC" (ticker HSBC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "HSBC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: HSBC Holdings plc
result.industry: Global universal banking and wealth management
markets: Hong Kong retail and commercial banking
UK ring-fenced retail and commercial banking
Global transaction banking (payments, cash management, trade finance)
Corporate and institutional banking and markets
International wealth management and premier banking
Insurance and asset management in Asia

mission.statement: Opening up a world of opportunity
mission.source: HSBC purpose statement, hsbc.com 'Our strategy and values' page
mission.plain: HSBC wants to help people and businesses use banking to reach chances and markets across the world.

about.plain: HSBC is one of the world's biggest banks, started in Hong Kong in 1865 and now based in London. It keeps people's savings, lends money for homes and businesses, and helps companies send money and goods between countries. Its biggest home markets are Hong Kong and the UK, and it is especially strong at helping customers who need banking in more than one country. It also helps richer customers invest and save in Asia.
about.customers: Millions of everyday savers and borrowers in Hong Kong and the UK, wealthy families in Asia, and companies and investors that trade around the world.
about.everyday: If you have used an HSBC or First Direct current account, a Hang Seng Bank card in Hong Kong, or seen the red-and-white hexagon logo at airports, that is HSBC.

money.plain: Payments, trade finance, loans and markets trading for companies and investors
Accounts, mortgages, cards and business loans in Hong Kong (HSBC and Hang Seng Bank)
Investments, insurance and private banking for well-off customers, mainly in Asia
Current accounts, mortgages and business loans in the UK (HSBC UK, First Direct)
Apps like Zing and Global Money for sending and holding money in many currencies

result.summary: HSBC has a real but bank-sized advantage: its dense international network in about 60 markets, leading position in Hong Kong and big UK deposit base give it cheap, sticky funding and hard-to-copy cross-border transaction banking. These advantages earn a mid-to-high-teens return on tangible equity in good years, but banking remains regulated, capital-intensive and rate-sensitive, so the moat is moderate rather than wide.

pricingPower.evidence: Banking NII rose to $44.1bn in 2025 and is guided to at least $46bn for 2026 even as rates fell, helped by low-cost Hong Kong deposits and structural hedges; but loan and deposit pricing is set largely by central-bank rates and competition, and fee pricing is regulated in the UK.

moats.evidence: HSBC is one of the most recognised bank brands globally and the trusted incumbent in Hong Kong since 1865, but bank brands rarely command premium pricing and reputations were dented by the 2012 money-laundering settlement.

Multinational clients embed HSBC's cash-management, payments and trade-finance platforms across dozens of countries, and retail customers' salaries, mortgages and direct debits make moving banks a hassle.
Its presence on both ends of trade and payment corridors (e.g. Asia, Middle East, Europe) makes it more useful to each client as more counterparties bank with it, a limited but real network effect.

With $3.4 trillion of assets at June 2026 and very large low-cost deposit bases in Hong Kong and the UK, HSBC funds itself cheaply, though its 2025 costs of $36.4bn on $68.3bn of revenue show no exceptional efficiency.

Hong Kong banking is concentrated in a few players (HSBC/Hang Seng, Bank of China Hong Kong, Standard Chartered), and HSBC is also one of the banks that issue Hong Kong dollar banknotes, limiting room for new entrants.
HSBC is the incumbent; digital challengers such as Revolut and Wise counter-position against it rather than the reverse.
Long experience in trade finance and cross-border compliance is valuable, but banking processes are widely copied and HSBC has had well-publicised compliance failures.
Banking licences in about 60 markets, a note-issuing role in Hong Kong and a decades-old client franchise in Asia are difficult for rivals to replicate.

customers.evidence: Deposits and corporate relationships are very sticky, but UK customer-satisfaction surveys typically rank HSBC UK mid-table (well behind First Direct, which HSBC also owns), and Hong Kong customers remain loyal largely through habit and network.

talent.evidence: HSBC is a well-known global graduate employer with about 211,000 staff (June 2025), but repeated restructuring and job cuts under the 2024-26 simplification programme weaken its appeal relative to top US investment banks.

product.evidence: HSBC is regularly ranked among the leaders in trade finance and global cash management (e.g. Euromoney awards), but its retail apps and products are not generally seen as best in class versus digital banks.

marketShare.market: Revenue of HSBC and Standard Chartered (the two big London-listed international banks focused on Asia)
marketShare.measure: share of combined reported FY2025 revenue/operating income ($89,216M), calculated from each bank's FY2025 results

threats: Falling interest rates in Hong Kong, the UK and the US squeezing net interest income on its large deposit base
Hong Kong and mainland China commercial real-estate credit losses (2026 ECL guided at about 45bps of loans)
US-China geopolitical tension and sanctions risk straddling its two most important markets
Digital challengers (Revolut, Wise) and Chinese state banks eroding retail and cross-border payment margins
Regulatory and conduct fines, and capital demands (CET1 fell to 14.1% after the $13.7bn Hang Seng Bank privatisation)
Execution risk in the restructuring into four businesses and exits from non-strategic markets

ceo.name: Georges Elhedery
ceo.background: Engineering degree from École Polytechnique and postgraduate degree in statistics and economics from ENSAE; joined HSBC in 2005 as a markets trader, later Global Head of Markets and Group CFO (2023-24)

c1.evidence: HSBC leads mature banking markets (Hong Kong, international transaction banking) rather than an emerging, fast-growing industry; 2025 revenue grew 3.7% to $68.3bn.

c2.evidence: Multinational clients choose HSBC for its network across about 60 markets and trade-finance expertise, which is hard to copy, but on most products it competes on price with many similar banks.

c3.evidence: HSBC is a household name worldwide and the default bank in Hong Kong, but it is not seen as a must-have product that customers enthusiastically recommend.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Opening up a world of opportunity' is repeated in reports, but management communication centres on returns (RoTE of 17% or better for 2026-2028), costs and capital.

c6.evidence: “big, global, traditional, Hong Kong bank”: the impression is mixed, positive on size and safety but tempered by past money-laundering fines, branch closures and job cuts.

c7.evidence: Global banking, cross-border payments and Asian wealth pools are huge and Asian wealth is growing, but banking overall grows roughly with nominal GDP.

c8.evidence: HSBC is expanding in Asian wealth (India, mainland China, Middle East) and digital payments such as Zing, but it is shrinking elsewhere by exiting non-strategic markets.

m1.evidence: Elhedery has a clear plan (simpler four-business structure, focus on international clients) but it is an efficiency strategy rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Elhedery is a career HSBC executive appointed CEO in September 2024, not a founder, and his agenda is driven by near-term return targets.

m4.evidence: There is no clear evidence either way; his tenure has featured large job cuts and $1.5bn of organisational simplification savings.

m5.evidence: His culture changes focus on speed and accountability ('We get it done'), not on inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: He holds an engineering degree from École Polytechnique and a statistics/economics degree from ENSAE, but his career is in markets trading and finance, not technology.

m7.evidence: No controversies attach to him personally; he sits on advisory boards such as the China Children Development Fund, but there is little public evidence on character beyond that.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Elhedery giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Elhedery is seen as a decisive but conventional banker, without a widely known public persona.

m9.evidence: In two years he completed the four-business reorganisation, the $13.7bn Hang Seng Bank privatisation and many exits, and 1H26 RoTE rose to 18.2% with profit before tax up to $19.5bn from $15.8bn; Euromoney named him Banker of the Year 2026.

m10.evidence: Cost discipline is central (2026 target-basis cost growth guided at about 1%, $1.5bn simplification savings), but HSBC is not known for a frugal culture.

c10.evidence: HSBC moves money, trade and savings for tens of millions of people and businesses worldwide, an essential but commodity-like service rather than a life-changing product.

p2.evidence: Running a compliant, safe global bank across about 60 jurisdictions is hard and important to world trade, but many large banks offer similar services.

f2.evidence: Profit before tax as a share of revenue rose from 17.4% in 2020 ($8,777M on $50,429M) to 43.8% in 2025 ($29,907M on $68,274M), though it dipped from 49.1% in 2024.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity is positive ($197,081M total equity at June 2026) and cash at central banks of $227,800M exceeds debt securities plus subordinated liabilities of $132,899M, but like any bank it is highly leveraged on total assets of $3.44 trillion.

f4.evidence: Profit before tax rose from $8,777M in 2020 to $29,907M in 2025 but fell from $32,309M in 2024; operating cash flow is volatile for a bank ($65,305M in 2024, $29,766M in 2025).

v1.evidence: No ordinary customer would say HSBC is clearly the best bank; its main edge is international reach for people and companies that bank across borders.

v2.evidence: HSBC is not generally listed among top employers in rankings such as Glassdoor's Best Places to Work, and repeated job cuts weigh on its reputation as an employer.

c5.evidence: If HSBC vanished overnight, Hong Kong's financial system, UK customers and global trade-finance clients would be badly disrupted for a while, but other banks would eventually take over its role.
